topic: Bayes' Theorem and the Logic of Independence
target_audience: Undergraduate students or advanced high school students

outline.topic: Bayes' Theorem and the Logic of Independence
outline.target_audience: Undergraduate students or advanced high school students

sections.title: Introduction: The Intuition of Independence
sections.content: Define 'Independence' as the scenario where one event occurring does not change the probability of another. Visually represent this using a 'Probability Square' where the area of intersection equals the product of individual side lengths.
sections.example: Flipping a coin while a cat meows. The cat meowing doesn't change the 50% chance of heads; these are independent events.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Conditional Probability & The Shrinking Universe
sections.content: Introduce P(A|B) — the probability of A occurring *given* B has happened. Graphically, show the 'Sample Space' (a large rectangle) shrinking to only the area of 'Event B'. The new probability is the 'A and B' intersection divided by the 'B' area.
sections.example: In a deck of cards, the probability of drawing a King is 4/52. But if we *know* the card is a Face Card (Event B), our 'universe' shrinks to 12 cards, making the probability 4/12.

sections.title: The Core: Deriving Bayes' Theorem
sections.content: Explain that Bayes' Theorem is just a way to 'flip' conditional probability. Use an animation to show the relationship between P(A|B) and P(B|A). Present the formula: P(A|B) = [P(B|A) * P(A)] / P(B). Highlight that this is how we update our beliefs based on new evidence.
sections.example: A 'Robot Sentry' sees a blurry shape. It knows the 'Prior' (how likely a thief is) and the 'Likelihood' (how often a thief looks like that shape) to calculate the 'Posterior' (the chance it's actually a thief).

sections.title: Step-by-Step Application: The Rare Dragon Test
sections.content: Apply the theorem to a classic 'False Positive' scenario using a flow-chart or tree diagram. This demonstrates why a positive test result doesn't always mean the condition is present, especially if the base rate (prior) is low.
sections.example: A Dragon-Detector is 99% accurate. Dragons are rare (1 in 1,000). If the alarm sounds, Bayes' Theorem shows there is only a ~9% chance it's a real dragon, because the 1% false alarm rate on 999 non-dragons outweighs the 99% true hit on 1 dragon.

sections.title: Conclusion: Independence vs. Bayesian Updating
sections.content: Summarize the key difference: Independence means new information is irrelevant. Bayes' Theorem proves that when events *are* dependent, new evidence allows us to update our certainty mathematically. End with a visual recap of the 'Probability Square' vs. the 'Shrinking Universe'.
sections.example: If the Dragon-Detector alarm is independent of dragons (it's broken), the probability remains 1/1,000. Because it's dependent, we use Bayes to update our 1/1,000 belief to 9%.

storyboard.title: Introduction: The Intuition of Independence
lecture_lines: Independence means one event doesn't affect another's probability.
A cat meowing doesn't change a coin flip's outcome.
We represent this visually using a probability square.
animations: Display two separate circles, labeled 'Event A' (#ADD8E6) and 'Event B' (#FFB6C1), on the left and right.
Move 'Event B' closer to 'Event A' but keep them non-overlapping. Change 'Event A' color to a brighter blue (#00BFFF) to highlight independence.
Display the text "Independent events do not affect each other" (#FFFFFF) below the circles.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: Conditional Probability & The Shrinking Universe
lecture_lines: Conditional probability looks at events within a restricted universe.
Imagine our sample space is a large rectangle.
If event B occurs, the universe shrinks to B.
Now, we only care about A within this new space.
The probability is the intersection divided by event B.
animations: Show a large rectangle representing the sample space 'S' (#D3D3D3) and a circle 'B' (#FFB6C1) inside it.
Scale 'S' down to match the size of 'B', visually "shrinking the universe" to 'B'.
Introduce a small area 'A' (#ADD8E6) overlapping with 'B', and label the intersection as 'A and B' (#00FF00).

storyboard.title: The Core: Deriving Bayes' Theorem
lecture_lines: Bayes' Theorem allows us to flip conditional probabilities.
We relate P(A given B) to P(B given A. )
This formula helps us update beliefs with new evidence.
It combines our prior knowledge with new likelihood data.
P(A|B) equals P(B|A) times P(A) divided by P(B).
animations: Display the equation P(A and B) = P(A|B) * P(B) in the center (#FFFFFF).
Below it, display the symmetric equation P(A and B) = P(B|A) * P(A) (#FFFFFF).
Animate an equals sign between P(A|B) * P(B) and P(B|A) * P(A), highlighting both terms in yellow (#FFFF00).
Fade out the shared P(A and B) part and move the right side terms to form a single equality.
Rearrange terms to show P(A|B) = [P(B|A)P(A)] / P(B), putting a bright box (#00FF00) around it.

storyboard.title: Step-by-Step Application: The Rare Dragon Test
lecture_lines: Consider a rare dragon with a 99% accurate detector.
Only one in a thousand creatures is a dragon.
If the alarm sounds, is it definitely a dragon?
Most positive results are actually false alarms from non-dragons.
Bayes shows the real chance is only nine percent.
animations: Display "P(Dragon) = 0.01" (#FFD700) on the left side of the screen.
Display "P(Positive | No Dragon) = 0.05" (#FFB6C1) below the first two.
Show the total probability calculation for "P(Positive)" appearing step-by-step (#FFFFFF).
Substitute all values into Bayes' formula and calculate the final result, "P(Dragon | Positive) ≈ 0.167", highlighted in bold (#00FF00).

storyboard.title: Conclusion: Independence vs. Bayesian Updating
lecture_lines: Independence means new information doesn't change our beliefs.
Dependence allows us to update certainty using Bayes' Theorem.
Use these tools to master the logic of probability.
animations: Show a graphic of a "Prior" belief (#FFD700) shifting to a "Posterior" belief (#00FF00) as "Evidence" (#ADD8E6) is added.
Pulse the final Bayes' Theorem formula in the center of the screen (#FFFFFF).
Fade out all elements and display a final "Thank You" message (#FFFFFF).
